article.intro: All the original text lives in English files alongside the code that uses it. Translations are generated automatically and stored separately. The same system handles everything from page content and validation errors to API responses and emails. There's no manual translation workflow and no language-specific logic in individual components.
article.switcher_caption: The language switcher, with each language's current status. Picking a language here loads the greeting in that language without changing the rest of the page.

why.title: Why I built it
why.rule: I wanted to make internationalization a property of the system rather than something each page or component had to implement.
why.intro: That meant setting a few rules before writing the code:
why.source: English is the source of truth. Every string lives in an English locale file and is referenced by key.
why.backend: The same translation system handles frontend content and backend messages, including validation errors, API responses and emails.
why.platform: Language negotiation uses the browser's `Accept-Language` header. There's no need for a separate cookie, query parameter or custom header to maintain the same information.
why.complete: A page always uses one language. If a translation isn't complete, the system falls back to the next language in the reader's preferences rather than mixing languages.
why.no_code: Adding a language or changing a string shouldn't require changes to application components.

how.title: How it works
how.browser: The browser already tells the server which languages the reader prefers. It sends an `Accept-Language` header with each request, ordered by preference and optionally weighted with quality values.
how.select: The API uses that information to select the first language with a complete translation. It returns the selected language in the `Content-Language` response header.
how.parts: The implementation has three main parts:
how.part_files: **English locale files** – the source strings, maintained alongside the application code.
how.part_mongodb: **MongoDB** – stores the English source and generated translations, one record per string and language.
how.part_job: **Translation job** – finds missing or outdated translations and generates them using Gemini, OpenAI or Groq.
how.startup: At startup, the API loads the translations from MongoDB into memory. The English locale files are seeded into the database, and a scheduled job handles the remaining languages.
how.source: When the English source changes, its stored copy no longer matches the translated record. The next translation run picks up that string and regenerates it. Unchanged translations are left alone.

negotiation.title: Language negotiation
negotiation.header_intro: An `Accept-Language` header might look like this:
negotiation.entries: Each entry represents a language preference. The optional `q` value indicates its priority, from 1 (highest) to 0 (unacceptable).
negotiation.list: The API parses the header, sorts the preferences by quality value, removes entries with `q=0`, and matches the remaining languages against those supported by the site. `en-US` is always added as the final fallback.
negotiation.matching: Language matching uses `Intl.Locale` to account for script and region differences. For example:
negotiation.match_exact: `es-MX` prefers Mexican Spanish when that translation is complete.
negotiation.complete: Only fully translated languages are eligible. If Mexican Spanish is still being generated, a request for `es-MX` falls back to the next available language in the preference list.
negotiation.note: The last example is worth noting: French isn't considered because `q=0` explicitly excludes it.

serving.title: Serving the selected language
serving.once: The API works out the language list once per request, in a middleware, and stores it in an `AsyncLocalStorage` for the rest of that request. Any code that runs while the request is handled can read it without the list being passed through every function call.
serving.backend: This is what lets the backend translate its own messages. A resolver can throw `translate('api', 'error_user_not_found')` without knowing which language the reader prefers. Validation errors, the Image Agent's fixed replies and emails work the same way. Work that carries on after the request returns, such as the Image Agent drawing a picture, keeps the language list of the request that started it.
serving.query: The `Translations` query returns every string for the namespaces a page asks for, in the first eligible language, and names that language in the `Content-Language` response header. The page starts in the language the API selected, so the language switcher always shows the language being displayed.
serving.header_only: The language is never sent in a request body. The API client sets the `Accept-Language` header itself, with the page's current language first and the browser's preferences after it. Choosing a language in the switcher changes that header and nothing else.

translating.title: Translation
translating.job: Translations are generated by a script, `make translations.translate`, which a GitHub workflow runs every day. It works through each language and namespace and only sends strings that are missing or whose English source has changed.
translating.prompt: The model receives one namespace's strings as JSON in a single request, along with the namespace and each string's key. The keys carry useful context: `action_send` is a button label and `error_user_not_found` is an error message. The prompt asks for a plain tone and a length close to the English.
translating.tokens: Some parts of a string have to come back exactly as they were sent:
translating.token_references: references to other strings, such as `$t(links.github)`
translating.checks: The job checks every response. If a string doesn't match, it retries that string once, then leaves it out if it still fails. Those strings are tried again on the next run.
translating.size: A whole namespace fits in one request because the limit that matters is the reply, not the request. Gemini accepts about a million tokens but returns at most 65,536, and a translation usually runs longer than the English. The largest namespace is about 36,000 tokens in English, and the languages I measured came back up to 27% longer. If a reply is cut off anyway, it can't be parsed as JSON, so the job splits those strings in half and sends each half again.
translating.plurals: Plural rules also differ between languages. English has two plural forms, Japanese has one and Arabic has six. The job asks for the forms each language needs, using the plural categories `Intl.PluralRules` reports for it, and the API uses the same rules to choose between them.
translating.notes: A language's name doesn't always say how it should be written. Traditional Chinese on this site follows the standard written Chinese used in Hong Kong rather than spoken Cantonese, so its record in `locales` carries a note that the prompt includes.
translating.providers: Requests go to Gemini first, then OpenAI, then Groq, using the same failover as the Image Agent. What happens when one refuses depends on the limit it reports. A per-minute limit refills on its own, so that model is skipped until it does, and if every model is waiting, the job waits too. A daily limit passes the work to the next model. When every model is out for the day, the run stops and the next one continues where it left off. Running out of quota isn't treated as a failure.

availability.title: Language availability
availability.complete: A language becomes available only when it has a translation for every string. The check compares it with the English source and ignores plural suffixes, because Chinese uses one plural form where English uses two.
availability.run: While the job is translating a language, it keeps a record of the run in MongoDB and updates it before each namespace. A record that hasn't been updated for five minutes is treated as a run that stopped without cleaning up.
availability.switcher: The language switcher subscribes to the status of every language. Complete languages can be selected. Incomplete ones are disabled and show a warning icon, or a spinner while they're being translated. A language becomes available within about a minute of its last string being written.
availability.adding: Adding a language is a data change. `make locales.add TAG=it-CH` adds a record to the `locales` collection, the next translation run fills in every string, and the language becomes available once it's complete. Its name in the switcher comes from `Intl.DisplayNames`, so nothing else has to be written.
availability.batch: The completeness rule makes large additions awkward. Adding hundreds of English strings to production would make every available language incomplete until they were translated, and readers would get English in the meantime.
availability.batch_order: So a large batch goes through a development database first. The strings are seeded and translated there, and the translations are copied to production before the English. By the time production counts the new strings, the translations are already in place, so no language drops out. Only the languages that are already available have to be ready, because the others are hidden anyway.

rtl.title: Right-to-left languages
rtl.intro: Arabic reads from right to left, so translating its words isn't enough. The page has to mirror too.
rtl.dir: Most of that comes from the browser. When the language changes, the site sets `dir` on the `<html>` element. The design system writes spacing and position with logical properties such as `margin-inline-start` rather than `left` or `right`, so rows reverse and text moves to the other edge without any code written for Arabic.
rtl.gaps: That covers the layout, but not everything on the page. When I went through the site in Arabic, a few things were still wrong.
rtl.arrows: `dir` changes the order of things, but it doesn't redraw an icon. Arrows kept pointing right, so the breadcrumb pointed backwards.
rtl.arrows_fix: Icons that point along the reading direction now use a `kicl-rtl-mirror` class, which flips them on right-to-left pages. Media controls stay as they are, because playback doesn't follow reading direction.
rtl.switch: The switch moved its thumb with `translate`, which only knows left and right, so in Arabic the thumb slid out of its track. It now moves with `margin-inline-start`, which follows the page's direction.
rtl.code: Code reads left to right in every language, but it was inheriting the page's direction. Punctuation ended up at the wrong end of each line, so `pre` and `code` now always run left to right.
rtl.flags: A flag emoji counts as a left-to-right character. In the language menu, that put Arabic's flag on the opposite side from every other row. Putting each name in a `bdi` element keeps it separate from the flag, so the flag lands on the same side in every row.
rtl.calendar: The calendar's grid mirrored on its own, but its arrow keys didn't, so pressing Left moved to the day on the right. The keys now check the page's direction first.
rtl.calendar_language: Its month and weekday names came from the browser's language, so an Arabic page could show English months. They now use the page's language.
rtl.english: The design system's docs were written in MDX files that the translation job never read, so the Arabic pages showed English sentences with their periods at the wrong end. That text now lives in the database and is translated like everything else.

implementation.title: See the implementation
implementation.code: The API, the translations in MongoDB and the translation job live in [Ki.CL-back]($t(common:url_api)). The frontend side, which loads each page's strings and follows `Content-Language`, lives in [Ki.CL]($t(common:url_host)).

wrong.title: What went wrong
wrong.every_request: My first approach was to translate each response as it was sent. That would have put a model call between every visitor and every page, added cost to a query that runs before a session exists, and given the same button different wording from one page load to the next. Translating once, when the English source changes, avoids all three problems.
wrong.mixed: Originally, each missing string fell back to English on its own, so a French page could contain an English sentence. With Arabic selected and nothing translated yet, the layout switched to right-to-left around English text. That's why a language now has to be complete before it can be used.
wrong.lost: Calling `translate()` directly returned French, but the same request over HTTP came back in English. The middleware was setting the language, but the resolvers never saw it.
wrong.lost_cause: The resolvers were loaded with `require()`, which gave them a second copy of every module, including a second `AsyncLocalStorage` that nothing wrote to. Loading them with `import()` fixed it. It also fixed a translation cache the resolvers had been loading separately instead of using the one filled at startup.
wrong.plurals: The first completeness check compared string keys exactly. Chinese has no `_one` plural form, so it could never match every English key, no matter how much of it had been translated.
wrong.quota: The job kept stopping with a message about quota, so I assumed the free tiers were used up and that translating everything would take days. The log said otherwise: Gemini was asking for a wait of about a second.
wrong.quota_cause: Gemini words a per-minute limit much like a spent daily quota, so the failover set the model aside for 30 minutes over that one-second wait. A per-minute limit on Groq then ended the run. The job was also making far more requests than it needed, because strings went out a few thousand characters at a time to fit a 30-second timeout. The largest namespace took 36 requests per language.
wrong.quota_fix: Per-minute limits now wait instead, and each namespace goes in one request.

limits.title: Limits
limits.review: Every translation is generated by a model and published without human review. A wrong translation can be fixed by editing its record, and the fix stays until the English source changes.
limits.variants: Each regional variant, such as Canadian French, needs a complete translation of its own.
limits.switching: The page selects its language when it loads. If a preferred language becomes available while you're reading, the page switches to it on the next load.
limits.html: The page title and description in the HTML, which search engines and link previews read, are always in English. The server fills them in the same way for every visitor.
limits.rtl: Arabic is the only right-to-left language on the site, so it's the only one I've tested.
limits.examples: Text inside the design system's live examples stays in English, because it has to match the code shown under it.

overview.title: How a sentence gets to you
overview.description: The browser sends Accept-Language to the API, and the API answers with Content-Language. The API reads every translation from MongoDB into memory. The English files are seeded into MongoDB. The translate job reads the strings a language is missing from MongoDB, sends them to Gemini, OpenAI or Groq, and writes the answers back.
overview.line_mongodb: One row per string and language

direction.title: What dir does and doesn't cover
direction.description: Setting dir on the html element makes the browser mirror rows and columns, text alignment and logical spacing. It doesn't reach arrows, the switch's thumb, code, flags in the language menu or the calendar's arrow keys, which the site had to fix itself.

limits.title: What happens to a request
limits.description: The translate job sends one namespace to the models, tried in order. A complete reply is checked and stored. A reply that's cut off is split in half and sent again. A per-minute limit skips that model until it refills, and the job waits if every model is waiting. A daily limit moves on to the next model, and the run stops when every model is out.

release.title: How a large batch ships
release.description: On the development database, the English is seeded and then translated. On production, the translations are copied first and the English second, so every available language stays complete. The code that reads the new strings is released last.
